observation_summary: The Closure Compiler's type checker fails to recognize JSDoc annotations (e.g., @param) on functions assigned to namespace properties when those functions are defined within a local scope (IIFE/module pattern). The failing tests verify that properties like 'goog.foo' and 'x.foo' should have declared function types, but the type checker treats them as if annotations were missing, emitting incorrect warnings.
hypothesis: The TypedScopeCreator.visit() method contained a custom switch statement handling FUNCTION, CATCH, and VAR tokens, but this logic incorrectly returned early for FUNCTION nodes whose parent was a NAME token, skipping the proper type declaration processing. This caused functions defined in local scopes and assigned to qualified names (e.g., ns.a = function() {}) to not have their JSDoc annotations registered in the type registry.
prediction: The buggy code would show a visit() method with a switch on node type that handles FUNCTION by checking if parent is NAME and returning early, thereby bypassing defineDeclaredFunction() for locally-scoped function assignments. The fix would replace this custom logic with a delegation to the parent ScopeCreator's visit() method, which correctly processes all declaration types including functions in nested scopes.
experiment_rationale: The unified diff confirms the hypothesis: the buggy version had a 21-line switch block handling FUNCTION/CATCH/VAR with an early return for FUNCTION when parent is NAME, while the fixed version replaces this entirely with 'super.visit(t, n, parent);'. This demonstrates the root cause was an incorrect local algorithm for AST traversal — the custom logic failed to handle the module pattern case, and delegating to the parent class's proven algorithm corrects the procedure.
reasoning_summary: This is an Algorithm/Method defect because the fix replaces an incorrect computational procedure (custom switch-based node visitation logic) with a correct one (delegation to parent class). The bug was not a missing guard (Checking), wrong value (Assignment/Initialization), interface mismatch (Interface/O-O Messages), timing issue (Timing/Serialization), cross-entity association (Relationship), or missing design capability (Function/Class/Object) — it was specifically a flawed local algorithm in the visit() method that mishandled FUNCTION nodes in nested scopes. The diff shows a pure algorithmic rewrite at the method level.
